cards.front: What precondition must be satisfied before binary search can be used?
cards.back: The data must already be sorted into order by the key being searched.

cards.explanation: Discarding half the list is only valid if being greater than the middle item guarantees the target is not in the lower half.

cards.back: Compare the target with the middle item of the current range. If it matches, stop. Otherwise discard the half that cannot contain the target and repeat on the remaining half, stopping when the target is found or the range is empty.

keyPoints.text: discard the half that cannot contain the target
repeat until found or the range is empty

cards.explanation: Each step halves the search space, which is where the O(log n) complexity comes from.

cards.front: What is the maximum number of comparisons binary search needs on a sorted list of 1024 items?
cards.explanation: Each comparison halves the range, so the answer is log2(1024) = 10. The 512 answer comes from halving once instead of repeating.

cards.front: Why is linear search still useful when binary search is faster?
cards.back: Linear search works on unsorted data and on structures that can only be read sequentially, such as a linked list or a data stream, where jumping to the middle item is not possible.

keyPoints.text: works where random access is not available

cards.explanation: Binary search needs the middle element in constant time, so an array is fine but a linked list would cost O(n) to reach it, removing the advantage.
